R03.construction: Reconstructed record. Compiled from the ESO technical report (Table 1 NGET/MeteoGroup rows and section 4.1), the NGET report in Appendix C (sections 1.1, 1.2, 2.2, 3.1-3.5, 4.1), the ESO answers to E3C questions in Appendix M (Q30) and Ofgem 3.18. Sections A-F restate published record values; ESO Table 1 times are written as ISO-8601 BST (+01:00) because the ESO executive summary dates the event at 4:52pm, while times whose clock basis no source states (section B2, section E) are kept as printed without an offset. The R03 clock line says that the B3/section C BST reading is an inference from that 4:52pm anchor and that only times without such an anchor are marked 'clock basis not stated' (the ESO 4.1 time 16:50:44 for Blyth-Eccles-Stella West has no anchor and conflicts with the Appendix M time 16:43:25, so both stay unlabelled in section E). Section D keeps measured magnitudes only; interpretations and compliance judgements (NGET, ESO, Ofgem) are in section G, in the assessing party's own wording. Section E lists both published times for the Blyth-Eccles-Stella West trip, which conflict, without resolving them; since bundle 1.1.0 there is no compiler's note pointing out the conflict (readers compare the two times themselves). Generator trips, frequency landmarks and demand disconnection are deliberately excluded.
R03.label: RECONSTRUCTED FOR EVALUATION FROM PUBLISHED RECORDS — NOT AN ORIGINAL SYSTEM EXPORT

R09.construction: Parts A-C quote and transcribe the ESO technical report (sections 6.2-6.4 and 7, Tables 8 and 9), Appendix M of its appendices, the E3C interim and final reports and Ofgem paragraph 3.23, every quotation and table cell checked on the stated PDF page (personal names in Table 8 replaced by roles). Part D indexes every held revision of the REMIT messages of T_HOWAO-1/2/3 and T_LBAR-1 (real Elexon data, unchanged; all fields in the CSV and the asset-log rows). Part E gives, for organisational posts and web statements, the decoded or displayed time and a gist written for this record (no gist shares more than three consecutive words with its source; not openly licensed). Part F quotes Ofgem and GOV.UK publications of 12-20 August 2019 (Open Government Licence). Ofgem's January 2020 enforcement settlements are excluded.

Part A heading
A1 ESO technical report section 6.2

sources.quote: The first communication between the ESO control room and BEIS was at 17:41hrs.
sources.section: 6.2 Engagement with government and the regulator

sources.quote: At this point the event was generally understood, demand restoration was in progress and further disturbances were considered unlikely.
sources.section: 6.2 Engagement with government and the regulator

sources.quote: The first communication with Ofgem was made at 17:51hrs with further communication at 18:17hrs and 18:45hrs and then throughout the weekend.
sources.section: 6.2 Engagement with government and the regulator

sources.quote: Further updates to BEIS from the ESO control room were made at 18:09hrs, 19:29hrs and 19:38hrs respectively.
sources.section: 6.2 Engagement with government and the regulator

segments.content: A2 ESO technical report section 7 (communications finding)

sources.quote: The ESO contacted BEIS at 17:40 and Ofgem at 18:00.
sources.section: 7. Report Findings

sources.quote: The initial media statement by the ESO issued at 18:27 with a subsequent statement at 20:06 and a video from the Head of National Control being posted at 20:11.
sources.section: 7. Report Findings

segments.content: A3 ESO appendices, Appendix M answers to E3C questions (Q34)

sources.quote: These answers are all based on the data available to the ESO on 28 August 2019.
sources.section: Appendix M – ESO E3C Questions and Answers

sources.quote: There appeared to be delays in escalations to Ofgem & BEIS after LFDD was initiated? Are there any lessons to be learnt?
sources.section: Appendix M, question 34

sources.quote: At 17:10hrs, the ENCC Power System Manager (PSM) reported the incident to the Head of National Control, ESO.
sources.section: Appendix M, question 34

sources.quote: The 1st communication between ENCC PSM and BEIS was at 17:41hrs.
sources.section: Appendix M, question 34

sources.quote: The 1st communication with Ofgem was made just after 18:00hrs with the Director of Operations, ESO.
sources.section: Appendix M, question 34

sources.quote: Further updates to BEIS from the PSM were made at 18:09hrs, 19:29hrs and 19:38hrs respectively.
sources.section: Appendix M, question 34

sources.quote: Current ESO procedure outlines that following an event of loss of supply, a clear communication to Ofgem & BEIS is essential.
sources.section: Appendix M, question 34

sources.quote: The communication is recommended to be initiated as soon as possible, and this procedure is in line with the ‘Energy Incident Reporting’ requirement set by Ofgem dated in December 2017.
sources.section: Appendix M, question 34

sources.quote: It is important in all cases that resolution of the incident remains the primary objective.
sources.section: Appendix M, question 34

B1 ESO section 6.3 and Table 8 (timeline of external communications)

sources.quote: The first ESO external communication was issued at 18:27hrs on 9 August.
sources.section: 6.3 External Communications with Media and Wider Industry

sources.quote: Table 8 provides the timeline of external communication with media and wider industry.
sources.section: 6.3 External Communications with Media and Wider Industry

sources.redaction: personal names replaced by the role in square brackets: Minister of State [name omitted]; [the Head of National Control]
sources.section: 6.3 External Communications with Media and Wider Industry, Table 8 – Timeline of external communications (continues on PDF page 31)

sources.quote: Table 8 – Timeline of external communications
sources.section: 6.3 Table 8 caption

segments.transformation: Table 8 rows as printed (day heading, time, event, distribution); personal names replaced by the role in square brackets.

segments.content: B2 ESO section 6.4 (media statements by others)

sources.quote: In the ~90 minutes immediately following the initial fault on the network (starting at 17.09hrs) statements were issued by some DNOs and rail companies stating that the loss of power and subsequent disruption was the result of a National Grid fault.
sources.section: 6.4 Communications by industry and consumers

sources.quote: These statements were issued ahead of any communication by the ESO and without engagement or coordination with the ESO communications team.
sources.section: 6.4 Communications by industry and consumers

sources.quote: These public-facing communications did not impact the speed with which the incident was resolved but did drive a large volume of media queries to the ESO.
sources.section: 6.4 Communications by industry and consumers

segments.content: B3 ESO appendices, Appendix M question 35

sources.quote: What issues did you encounter with the public-facing communications by industry, notably in terms of the content and timelines for the messaging?
sources.section: Appendix M, question 35

sources.quote: The initial communications from some DNOs and rail companies said that the incident had been caused by a National Grid fault.
sources.section: Appendix M, question 35

sources.quote: These communications were issued very shortly after the event (from 5.09pm onwards).
sources.section: Appendix M, question 35

sources.quote: The ESO prepared an external communication seeking to give reassurance to the public which was issued at 18:27 once it was established that the DNOs had reconnected all customers.
sources.section: Appendix M, question 35

sources.quote: The initial statements from some parts of the industry were issued before our statement and without any co-ordination with our comms team.
sources.section: Appendix M, question 35

segments.content: B4 E3C interim report (communications, post-event announcement)

sources.quote: DNOs led local public communications during the event and the ESO did not publish public statements until after the disruption, meaning that energy partners (such as generators) were not directly informed.
sources.section: communications

sources.quote: In parallel with social media, DNOs reached out to customers via text message alert services and telephone services between 17:02 and 18:30.
sources.section: communications

sources.quote: Updates from the ESO followed the first set of restorations and were not publicly released until 18:27 via Twitter.
sources.section: communications

sources.quote: The Secretary of State for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy later announced via Twitter (10th August) and GOV.UK (14th August) that the government was to commission the Energy Emergencies Executive Committee to provide an interim and extended report into the power disruptions.
sources.section: Post-event

segments.content: B5 E3C final report section 5 (communication channels)

sources.quote: The first public announcement from ESO was issued at 18:27, which was following the event and once the system had stabilised.
sources.section: 5. Communication channels

sources.quote: By this time, many DNOs had used twitter to provide area updates that were widely circulated.
sources.section: 5. Communication channels

sources.quote: However, electricity generators received no communication during the events of 9 August that would have made them aware of the system condition.
sources.section: 5. Communication channels

segments.content: B6 Ofgem report paragraph 3.23 (Hornsea 1 communication with the ESO)

sources.quote: We have also found issues with Hornsea 1’s communication with the ESO.
sources.section: paragraph 3.23

sources.quote: Hornsea 1 did not notify the ESO directly when the wind farm deloaded by 737MW.
sources.section: paragraph 3.23

sources.quote: The wind farm then began its process of starting up two of its modules (temporarily) without
sources.section: paragraph 3.23

sources.quote: any coordination with the ESO whilst the ESO was attempting to respond to the generation losses it was aware of.
sources.section: paragraph 3.23 (continued)

sources.quote: Analysis of the volume of calls to the 105 helpline provides a useful indicator of the scale of customer impact across the DNOs and the timeframe for disruption to power supplies with calls dropping off dramatically post 6pm.

segments.content: Part F heading
F1 Ofgem sets timeline for National Grid ESO report following UK power failures (press release, 12 August 2019)

sources.quote: Ofgem has written to the National Grid Electricity System Operator requesting an urgent interim report into the incident on 9 August 2019 to be provided to Ofgem by Friday 16 August.
A final, detailed technical report must be provided to Ofgem by Friday 6 September.

segments.content: F2 Business Secretary sets out scope of investigation into power cuts (press release, first published 2019-08-14T11:15:35+01:00)

sources.quote: National Grid has said power cuts had “nothing to do with changes in wind speed or the variability of wind”
The government today (14 August 2019) set out the scope of its review into the actions of the National Grid Electricity System Operator after Friday’s power cuts.
The committee met for the first time on Monday (12 August) and will provide a report on initial findings within 5 weeks to the Secretary of State for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy.
It will then submit a comprehensive report within 12 weeks.
This review will complement the investigation being undertaken by energy regulator Ofgem into how the electricity operator responded in line with its licence conditions and system security standards.

segments.content: F3 Great Britain power system disruption review (publication page; first published 2019-08-14T11:15:00+01:00, updated 2019-10-04 and 2020-01-03)

sources.quote: On Friday 9 August 2019 a power disruption resulted from the operation of Low Frequency Demand Disconnection relays on the Great Britain power system at about 4:54 pm.
Though demand was fully restored within 90 minutes, the secondary impacts continued to be felt for much of the day.

segments.content: F4 Ofgem launches investigation into power cuts (press release, 20 August 2019)

sources.quote: Ofgem has launched an investigation into the power cuts of Friday 9 August, following an initial report from National Grid Electricity System Operator (NGESO).

It will also seek to establish whether any of the parties involved – National Grid ESO, National Grid Electricity Transmission, 12* distribution network operators in England and Wales, as well as generators RWE Generation (Little Barford Power station) and Orsted (Hornsea) - breached their licence conditions.

Ofgem is liaising with the rail regulator (Office of Rail and Road) and will be engaging with the rail authorities to understand better why the drop in frequency on the energy network led to disruption for passengers.
The opening of this investigation does not imply that Ofgem has made any findings about non-compliance for any of the companies mentioned at this early stage of the investigation.

R10.construction: Reconstruction of requirements as the published reports describe them, item by item, for the LFDD, security-standard, response-product and distributed-generation questions of the system-response task. It is not code text: the handoff states that the Grid Code, SQSS and Distribution Code editions applicable on 9 August 2019 were not archived and verified, so each item names the report it restates and keeps differences between reports (e.g. infrequent infeed loss 1,260 MW in ESO 2.2 vs 1800 MW in the ESO glossary; LFDD up to 60% in Ofgem/E3C vs 'up to 40% available' in the ESO glossary). The 5% stage-1 requirement is given with its winter-peak / average-cold-spell basis exactly as Ofgem and the E3C state it. Full-investigation edition: lines 1-133 are the system-response R10 unchanged (byte-identical, so its line locators still resolve); Sections F-K are appended from builder/full_investigation/recon/text/R10_additions.src.txt and restate, item by item, the fault-ride-through and voltage-damping requirements Ofgem describes, the ESO's account of the generator compliance process, the reconnection and incident-notification arrangements as described, LFDD and essential services, and rail traction-supply frequency limits as ORR, GTR and Ofgem describe them. Clause numbers appear only where a report's footnote cites them; no ESQCR duty or OC7/OC10 obligation is restated (handoff T19), and ORR's 2.1 sentence attributing the 50 Hz +/-0.5 Hz range to the SQSS and the ESQCR is left out for that reason (the SQSS limits are already in Section A).

segments.content: Section heading
ESO 2.2: SQSS secured events and frequency limits

sources.quote: It specifies the limits of frequency deviations for secured events, which include loss of output from a single generating unit, Combined Cycle Gas Turbine Module (CCGT), boiler, nuclear reactor or DC bi-pole lost as a result of an event.
sources.section: 2.2 ESO Roles and Responsibilities – Principles of Managing Frequency

sources.quote: Normal Infeed Loss Risk: Maximum frequency deviation should not exceed 0.5Hz
sources.section: 2.2 ESO Roles and Responsibilities – Principles of Managing Frequency

sources.quote: Infrequent Infeed Loss Risk Frequency should not deviate outside the range 49.5Hz to 50.5Hz for more than 60 seconds.
sources.section: 2.2 ESO Roles and Responsibilities – Principles of Managing Frequency

segments.content: ESO 2.2: normal loss c. 1,000; infrequent 1,260 MW

sources.quote: The level of the normal infeed loss actually covered depends on the configuration of the system at the time (typically it is c. 1,000W). The current normal infrequent infeed maximum loss risk is 1,260MW for when Sizewell nuclear station is operating at full load.
sources.section: 2.2 ESO Roles and Responsibilities – Principles of Managing Frequency

segments.content: Appendix H: normal and infrequent infeed loss definitions

sources.quote: the maxiumim loss the system should be able to manage without the frequency going below 49.5 Hz (e.g., an interconnector at 1,000MW)
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

sources.quote: is a higher level of infeed loss dictated by a small number of larger potential losses (e.g., Sizewell at 1,260MW) and for the loss of which the frequency should not go below 49.2 Hz and should recover to 49.5 Hz within one minute.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

segments.content: Appendix H: N-1, single Secured Event; power infeed loss

sources.quote: The SQSS anticipates that only one Secured Event would happen at any one time and does not assume multiple Secured Events occurring simultaneously. In engineering terms this is defined as N-1
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

sources.quote: The Power Infeed Loss is the amount of power infeed that can be lost in one Secured Event.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

sources.quote: Generally this is either a single large generator, with a single mode of failure such as a single connection to the transmission system or could be two or more smaller generators that are separate but are connected to the rest of the system through an asset treated as a single Secured Event (for example a double circuit overhead line or busbar).
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

segments.content: Appendix H: re-securing

sources.quote: The SQSS also sets out that the system should be re-secured as soon as reasonably practicable after the occurrence of a Secured Event.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

segments.content: ESO glossary: infrequent infeed loss upper limit 1800 MW

sources.quote: The current maximum upper limit for an infrequent infeed loss risk is 1800MW.
sources.section: 9 Glossary of Terms

segments.content: Ofgem Box 4: 49.5 Hz or recovery within 60 s

sources.quote: Specifically, the SQSS requires frequency to stay above or equal to 49.5Hz or that any fall below that level should be recovered within 60 seconds for such events. The ESO is required to secure the system by holding reserves so that the frequency limits are not breached for these events.
sources.section: Ofgem Box 4: SQSS

segments.content: E3C final footnote 14

sources.quote: The SQSS allows for a deviation below 49.5Hz provided that the frequency is returned to 49.5Hz within 60 seconds.
sources.section: E3C final, footnote 14

segments.content: Ofgem 3.2 and 3.5: ESO position on DG losses under the SQSS

sources.quote: The ESO does not consider it is required to secure against distributed generation losses under the SQSS.
sources.section: Ofgem 3.2 and 3.5

sources.quote: The ESO follows an internal policy of only securing against both transmission-
sources.section: Ofgem 3.2 and 3.5

sources.quote: connected generation losses and distributed generation losses from vector shift protection mechanisms for credible transmission network faults during periods of increased risk to the transmission system (e.g. bad weather, lightning) or when it considers it economic to do so.
sources.section: Ofgem 3.2 and 3.5

segments.content: Section heading
Appendix H: RoCoF 0.125 Hz/s in largest-loss securing

sources.quote: In securing for the largest loss, the ESO also takes into account the known protection setting historically specified in the Distribution Code for RoCoF of 0.125 Hz/s.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

sources.quote: seeks to ensure that the system is configured in real-time such that the limit of 0.125Hz/s is not breached for an infeed loss.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

segments.content: ESO answer 11: RoCoF limit and containment limits

sources.quote: We also secure the system to within a ROCOF limit of 0.125 Hz/s for the largest credible loss.
sources.section: Appendix M – ESO E3C Questions and Answers (data available to the ESO on 28 August 2019), answer 11

sources.quote: We then schedule sufficient frequency response to ensure the largest loss is contained to frequency limits (49.5Hz for a normal loss, 49.2 Hz for an abnormal loss)
sources.section: Appendix M – ESO E3C Questions and Answers (data available to the ESO on 28 August 2019), answer 11

segments.content: Appendix H: ~2 GW on RoCoF relays

sources.quote: Approximately 2 GW of small generators are connected to the distribution networks via relays which disconnect the generators if the RoCoF is greater than 0.125Hz/s.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

segments.content: Appendix H: ~8.5 GW on vector shift relays

sources.quote: Approximately 8.5 GW of small generators are connected to the distribution networks via relays which disconnect the generators if the Vector Shift angle is greater than 6 degrees.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

segments.content: Appendix H: vector shift Type A and Type B

sources.quote: transmission faults with no coincident loss of BMU infeed (e.g. an overhead line)
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

sources.quote: transmission faults with coincident loss of BMU infeed (e.g. a generator busbar)
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

sources.quote: The ESO actively monitors, models and forecasts the largest Type A Vector Shift risk (e.g., associated with a fault on a transmission circuit) for each half-hourly settlement period
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

sources.quote: Type B faults are only secured based on it being economic to do so.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

segments.content: Section heading
Appendix H: primary response timing

sources.quote: It must be delivering it’s required output by 10 seconds following the trip and must continue to deliver for a further 20 seconds (30 seconds total)
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

segments.content: Appendix H: secondary response timing

sources.quote: It must be delivering it’s required output by 30 seconds following the change in frequency and must continue to deliver for a further 30 minutes.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

segments.content: Appendix H: dynamic and static

sources.quote: Dynamic - Is a continuously provided service to manage the normal fluctuations in the frequency.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

sources.quote: Static - Is a service to provide frequency response when the system frequency transgresses the low frequency relay setting on site.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

sources.quote: These two types of service can be provided from generation and demand, BM and Non-BM units.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

segments.content: Appendix H: mandatory and commercial response

sources.quote: Mandatory Frequency Response (MFR): This can only be provided by synchronised BM units. The requirement for MFR is an obligation of the Grid Code.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

sources.quote: Commercial response contracts: This is the service procured from generation or demand, BM or Non-BM units. The providers are required to deliver the contracted amount of response.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

segments.content: ESO answer 13: FFR, MFR, EFR, static

sources.quote: Firm Frequency Response (FFR): this is tendered for on a monthly basis
sources.section: Appendix M – ESO E3C Questions and Answers (data available to the ESO on 28 August 2019), answer 13

sources.quote: Mandatory Frequency Response: this has similar characteristics as FFR but is provided as an obligation laid out in a generator’s connection agreement
sources.section: Appendix M – ESO E3C Questions and Answers (data available to the ESO on 28 August 2019), answer 13

sources.quote: Enhanced Frequency Response (EFR): this is a faster form of FFR
sources.section: Appendix M – ESO E3C Questions and Answers (data available to the ESO on 28 August 2019), answer 13

sources.quote: This reduces demand or increases generation when the frequency hits a trigger limit
sources.section: Appendix M – ESO E3C Questions and Answers (data available to the ESO on 28 August 2019), answer 13

sources.quote: Short Term Operating Reserve: this service typically delivers energy within 20 minutes or less
sources.section: Appendix M – ESO E3C Questions and Answers (data available to the ESO on 28 August 2019), answer 13

sources.quote: Rapid Start: this provides access to energy in less than 2 minutes
sources.section: Appendix M – ESO E3C Questions and Answers (data available to the ESO on 28 August 2019), answer 13

sources.quote: Balancing Mechanism Actions
sources.section: Appendix M – ESO E3C Questions and Answers (data available to the ESO on 28 August 2019), answer 13

segments.content: Appendix H: minimum dynamic response 550 MW

sources.quote: To ensure the quality of steady state frequency control, a minimum amount of dynamic response must be held.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

sources.quote: The minimum dynamic response requirement at the time of the incident was set to 550MW.
sources.section: Appendix H – Managing Frequency with Statutory Limits

segments.content: Ofgem 3.38: OC6, max 60% at winter demand, tolerance and delay

sources.quote: The Grid Code (Operating Code 6) requires each DNO in England and Wales to have LFDD equipment in place to disconnect a maximum of 60% of demand (measured at winter demand). This equipment should operate in stages to disconnect a given percentage of supply once certain frequencies are reached. The Grid Code requirements contain an accuracy tolerance for the frequency levels and a time delay permitted for different LFDD equipment, depending on its installation date.
sources.section: Ofgem section 3, DNOs, 3.38

sources.quote: Generators that make use of the transmission networks are entitled to do so because they are signatories to the CUSC and have a connection agreement with National Grid ESO. The CUSC in turn places an obligation on generators to meet the requirements of the Grid Code, including any site-specific criteria in their connection agreement.
sources.section: 2.4 Generator Roles and Responsibilities

sources.quote: The Grid Code sets out a range of capabilities that a generator must have, including voltage control and frequency control. It is the Grid Code that states what a generator is expected to do during and after a network fault.

segments.content: E3C final chapter 1: CUSC and Grid Code capabilities

sources.quote: Generators that connect to the transmission network are required to comply with the Connection and Use of System Code7 and the Grid Code8. These documents set out the range of capabilities that a generator must have, including voltage control and frequency control, and what a generator is expected to do during and after a fault on the network.
sources.section: chapter 1, Loss of generation

segments.content: Section heading
ESO 2.4: compliance process; generators to assure themselves

sources.quote: The Grid Code also sets out an extensive process for new generators to demonstrate that they can meet certain requirements to enable safe connection. The details are set out in the CP (Compliance Process) section of the code. It is for the generators to assure themselves of their compliance with the Grid Code requirements.
sources.section: 2.4 Generator Roles and Responsibilities

segments.content: Appendix G: responsibilities and stage gates

sources.quote: Generators are responsible for demonstrating and maintaining compliance with the Grid Code both when connecting to the system initially and on an ongoing basis.
sources.section: Appendix G – Compliance Testing for Hornsea and Little Barford, Overview of the Compliance Testing Process

sources.quote: Compliance is demonstrated through a combination of studies, simulations and testing of the generator. The ESO runs the compliance process and supports the generator in achieving compliance. For the initial connection of any large[1] or directly connected generator, the generator proceeds through a number of stage gates in the process: energisation stage, interim operational stage and final operation stage. The generator must provide the required compliance evidence at each stage. The ESO is responsible for assessing this information against the Grid Code requirements and issues a notice to proceed through the stage gate if compliance has been met.
sources.section: Appendix G – Compliance Testing for Hornsea and Little Barford, Overview of the Compliance Testing Process

segments.content: Appendix G: notify changes; ESO not checking ongoing; LON after 84 days

sources.quote: If the generator makes any changes to its configuration which may impact compliance, it is responsible for firstly notifying the ESO of the change and then ensuring that it demonstrates compliance. The ESO is not responsible for checking compliance on an ongoing basis.
sources.section: Appendix G – Compliance Testing for Hornsea and Little Barford, Overview of the Compliance Testing Process

sources.quote: If a generator believes it would require more than 84 days to resolve any compliance issues, the ESO issues a Limited Operational Notice (LON) to the generator and work with them to achieve full compliance

segments.content: ORR 2.4: LFDD band; duty holder's back-up responsibility

sources.quote: 48.8 Hz is one of the low frequency demand disconnection (LFDD) bands where the Distribution Network Operator (DNO) sheds load to stabilise the system and to protect essential services such as the rail traction supply. segments.content: A2 Publisher's explanation of the columns (quotations)

sources.quote: The data contains both delay and cancellation events (denoted by the performance event code) and a user should be careful when summing delay minutes (pfpi minutes) to exclude cancellation events.

It is possible that the detailed reasons for some of the delays in this file are still being investigated and until this is complete the responsibility for the delay is still not finalised (see attribution status).
Delay data is remapped to reflect the franchise mapping at the time of the data extraction (in this case May 2021).
trainids are unique within a railway period but not within a year
Train schedule type / traction type/ trailing load / unit class – these aren’t mandated or validated fields within PSS
Incident number – the TRUST DA incident number (not unique without the create date)
Incident create date – the date the incident was entered into the system
Incident start/end date – the date the system has the incident live (this is not the length of the incident on the ground)
Responsible Manager – who within the industry is responsible for the delay – all delays have responsibility for performance improvement purposes
Incident Reason – the Delay Attribution Guide cause code for the incident
Incident equipment – internal free form information
Incident description – short description of the incident for internal use
If no code the delay is primary (ie the delay is at the site of the incident) if reactionary the delay is a later consequence of that incident
A and M denote delays, C, D, O, P, S and F are cancellations … C – is a full cancelletion, D is a diversion, F is a failure to stop, S is a scheduled cancellation and O/P are part cancellations
Start/end stanox – the location of the delay (not the incident)
Event Datetime – the time the train encountered the delay

Pfpi minutes – the size of the delay …. Note if the train is cancelled (performance event code) a deemed delay minute is generated for internal usage in these circumstances the train hasn’t been delayed and including this delay in any calculation of delay is misleading.
Applicable timetable flag – if N the train is not in official performance records as it is a short term replacement of a train plan – normally a reinstatement of part of a cancelled service

Causal statements and mechanisms (for example WTG overcurrent protection as the de-load mechanism, first established in the operator's 5 September report) appear only in the dated, attributed post-event annotations (Ørsted report 2019-09-05, ESO report 2019-09-06, Ofgem report 2020-01-03). S03.construction: Synthesised record. The sequence of events transcribes the RWE preliminary findings table (APP Appendix E, PDF page 45; event/offset pairing confirmed from the PDF's word positions): raw offsets from the datum T only. RWE states no clock basis for T = 16:52:34 +/- 0.5 s; the clock line says that T is read as BST (the ESO timeline lists the RWE-sourced steam turbine trip at 16:52:34) and keeps RWE's statement that T is not yet aligned with the ESO datum. Since bundle 1.1.0 the record gives no T + offset BST times, no intervals between entries and no arithmetic check of the station total; readers derive these themselves and carry the datum uncertainty. Unit outputs come from ESO Table 2; the 641 MW station total is the value published in ESO 4.2 and Ofgem 3.27. Causal statements appear only in the attributed annotation section dated 30 August 2019, in the operator's own wording and without builder labels. Nothing about other generators or frequency landmarks is included.

S04.construction: Synthesised account in two parts. Part 1 is a role-level, chronological shift narrative restating only published facts (ESO 4.2 Little Barford, the RWE SOE in APP Appendix E, Ofgem 3.25-3.29); no names, conversations, readings or clock times are added and no illustrative values are used. Part 2 gives attributed post-event statements, each in its source's order: the RWE preliminary findings dated 30 August 2019 (UPS, steam turbine, gas turbines) and Ofgem 3.28-3.29 dated 3 January 2020, as verbatim quotes or close paraphrase. Since bundle 1.1.0 the account carries no builder classification (no known/not known, established/not established or hypothesis labels); the sources' own words ('RWE's hypothesis is', 'is ongoing', 'For reasons presently unknown', 'We have established', 'has not been established', 'preliminary view') carry the epistemic status. Deliberately not carried into the pack (flagged for the domain reviewer, criteria D4.3/D4.4): the ESO executive summary (PDF page 4) says the GT1A trip was 'due to high pressure in the steam bypass system following the failure of a bypass valve to operate correctly'. ESO section 4.2 (PDF page 20) and RWE (APP page 46) give the excursion's cause as 'presently unknown', and Ofgem 3.29 states that the root cause of the high pressure conditions has not been established, so the pack keeps it unknown. A submission that asserts a bypass-valve failure as established is not supported by the visible evidence.
S04.label: SYNTHESISED FOR EVALUATION — NOT REAL EVIDENCE

segments.content: GTR event summary 1: frequency information supplied by National Grid

sources.quote: From information supplied by the National Grid at 1653 on Friday the 9th of August the frequency of the OLE AC voltage supply dropped below 49Hz for 16 seconds. It dropped below 48.89Hz to a minimum of 48.8 Hz for milliseconds.

sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Event Summary, item 2

segments.content: GTR event summary 3: protective shutdown of Class 700/717 4QC; other classes unaffected

sources.quote: All Desiro City class 700 and 717 units operating on AC Voltage suffered a Protective Shutdown where the converter, known as the 4QC (4 Quadrant Controller) shut down.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Event Summary, item 3

sources.quote: None of the other AC trains in the GTR fleet suffered any power related issues from this event e.g. Class 387, Class 365, Class 313.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Event Summary, item 3

segments.content: GTR event summary 4: circa 60 units

sources.quote: In Passenger Service this involved circa 60 units, consisting of Class 700 FLU/RLUs and Class 717, suffering a 4QC lock out.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Event Summary, item 4

segments.content: GTR event summary 5: train state on battery power

sources.quote: The effect of the 4QC shutting down on the train is that the train switches to battery power which causes a loss of HVAC (fan only fresh air supply), stand by reduced lighting (emergency lighting is activated when battery voltage drops), no at seat power, no PIS displays (audio only from the cab), and no traction power. The GSM-R radio remains active.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Event Summary, item 5

segments.content: GTR event summary 6: Battery Reset as first response, about 10 minutes

sources.quote: Following failed attempts to repower the trains, the established first response for a train failing with these symptoms is for the Driver to perform a reboot of the train known as a Battery Reset. This takes approximately 10 minutes.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Event Summary, item 6

segments.content: GTR event summary 7: Fleet Control diagnosis and GSM-R broadcast

sources.quote: Fleet Control diagnosed the issue quickly and a global GSM-R call was broadcast to instruct drivers to carry out the Battery Reset process.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Event Summary, item 7

segments.content: GTR event summary 8: 27 units recovered

sources.quote: After this 27 of the affected units were recovered.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Event Summary, item 8

segments.content: GTR event summary 9: circa 30 units needed a technician

sources.quote: The remaining circa 30 units required the Protective Shutdown to be unlocked by the intervention of a Technician with a laptop attending each unit.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Event Summary, item 9

segments.content: GTR event summary 10: 17 technicians plus 24 mobilised

sources.quote: There were 17 Technicians available at the time of the event. These 17 were immediately sent to stranded units with laptops and a further 24 technicians were mobilized within the next hour. The trains affected were widely spread geographically and some were not easily accessible.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Event Summary, item 10

segments.content: GTR event summary 11: 23 train evacuations

sources.quote: Therefore, this process took some time and resulted in 23 train evacuations and severe levels of service disruption.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Event Summary, item 11

segments.content: GTR cause 1: software-enabled train needs frequency-excursion protection

sources.quote: The Desiro City from Siemens Mobility is the latest generation software enabled commuter train, so requiring protection against power supply frequency excursions for safety reasons and to protect low power electronics.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Cause, item 1

segments.content: GTR cause 2: Siemens specification down to 48.5 Hz for short periods

sources.quote: Siemens Technical Specification for the train states that the train will continue to operate with supply frequency drops down to 48.5Hz for short periods of time.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Cause, item 2

segments.content: GTR cause 3: NR/GN/ELP/27010 identifies 48.5 Hz in extreme conditions

sources.quote: The NR Electrification System Compatibility document, NR/GN/ELP/27010 (“Guidance for compatibility between electric trains and electrification systems”), a Manufacturing and Supply Agreement compliance requirement, identifies that the supply frequency can fall to 48.5Hz in extreme conditions.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Cause, item 3

segments.content: GTR cause 4: NoBo design submission

sources.quote: A review of the Class 700 NoBo design submission (Siemens document A6Z00036309602 item 4.2.8.2.2) shows that compliance with both NR/GN/ELP 27010 and EN 50163
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Cause, item 4

segments.content: GTR cause 5: EN 50163 Clause 4.2 Note 2 and the 49 Hz design value

sources.quote: Siemens advised that the supply frequency response of the train was designed to comply with the EN 50163 Clause 4.2 Note 2. This note permits train drives to disconnected at 49Hz. Use of this supply frequency value in the train design led to the train protectively shutting down its drives when the supply frequency response fell below 49Hz.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Cause, item 5

segments.content: GTR cause 6: no Permanent Lockout intended; 30 trains not recoverable

sources.quote: Importantly Siemens have also clarified that there should not have been a Permanent Lockout on the train following a protective shutdown caused by a supply voltage frequency drop. All trains should have been recoverable via Battery Reset whereas 30 trains were not recoverable. This was not the intended behaviour of the train.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Cause, item 6

segments.content: GTR cause 7: not design intent; risk not known before

sources.quote: Therefore, the affected Class 700 and 717 sets did not react according to their design intent in these circumstances. The risk of this happening was not known prior to the power event on Friday 9 August.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Cause, item 7

segments.content: GTR cause 8: TCMS 3.27 removed battery-reset recovery from Permanent Lockout

sources.quote: Separately as a part of the new TCMS (Train Control Management System) software version 3.27, the ability for the driver to recover from a Permanent Lockout by using the Battery Reset process was removed.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Cause, item 8

segments.content: GTR cause 9: software levels of technician-recovered vs driver-recovered units

sources.quote: On the 9th of August all the units which required a Technician to recover power were at software level 3.27 or above. The 28 units recovered by the driver performing a Battery Reset were at the previous TCMS software level of 3.25 or below.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Cause, item 9

segments.content: GTR conclusion 1

sources.quote: All the Class 700 and Class 717 trains operating on AC suffered a Protective Shutdown of the 4QC controller because of a drop in the supply frequency below 49Hz for 16 seconds.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Conclusion, item 1

segments.content: GTR conclusions 2-4

sources.quote: This was not how the train system had been specified to operate. This event should not have caused a Permanent Lockout fault on the trains.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Conclusion, items 2 to 4

sources.quote: The effects of this were exacerbated as the fleet was undergoing a software change, contained in this was a change in functionality removing the Battery Reset remedy for Permanent Lockout events.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Conclusion, items 2 to 4

sources.quote: This meant that the driver could not recover failed trains which were operating on the new software, instead a Technician was required to attend.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Conclusion, items 2 to 4

segments.content: GTR planned mitigation 1: patch to recover above 49.5 Hz

sources.quote: Siemens are developing a software patch to allow units which protectively shutdown below 49Hz supply frequency to recover themselves without the need of a reboot or laptop when the frequency rises above 49.5Hz.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Planned Mitigation, item 1

segments.content: GTR planned mitigation 2: no reversion; excursion risk considered extremely unlikely

sources.quote: It is not proposed by Siemens or GTR to revert units to previous software versions as there are concerns this could severely impact unit availability. Based on discussions with the National Grid Head of Networks, the risk of frequency excursion dropping below 49Hz before the patch is fully introduced are considered extremely unlikely.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Planned Mitigation, item 2

segments.content: GTR planned mitigation 3: operation down to 48.5 Hz to be investigated

sources.quote: In addition to this Siemens will investigate how the train could be made to operate for a short time with supply frequency falling to 48.5Hz.
sources.section: Appendix F – Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) technical report, Planned Mitigation, item 3

segments.content: Part heading: ESO report date and the sections restated

sources.quote: Technical Report on the events of 9 August 2019 6 September 2019
sources.section: Title page

segments.transformation: Section numbers 5.2 and 7 are the ESO report's own; see the segments' section labels.

segments.content: ESO 5.2: Class 700/717 shutdowns north of Farringdon and Kings Cross

sources.quote: Class 700 and 717 trains shut down north of Farringdon and Kings Cross stations due to their internal protection systems being triggered. The Network Rail overhead line power supply operated continually. The shutdown of these trains had a knock-on impact by delaying all other trains behind them requiring the temporarily closure of London St Pancras and Kings Cross stations which led to Friday rush hour overcrowding.
sources.section: 5.2 Critical Infrastructure – Rail

segments.content: ESO 5.2: summary of GTR's report (approximately 60, half, 30)

sources.quote: The report sets out that all Desiro City Class 700 and Class 717 trains that were operating on AC power suffered a protective shutdown when the frequency deviation fell below 49Hz. Of the approximately 60 Class 700 and Class 717 trains that shutdown, half were restarted by the driver on site performing a reboot of the train, which takes c10mins. The remaining 30 trains required a technician to attend each train with a laptop to reset the trains.
sources.section: 5.2 Critical Infrastructure – Rail

segments.transformation: ESO prints 'c10mins'; written as 'c. 10 minutes'.

segments.content: ESO 5.2: GTR statement on specification and 48.5 Hz

sources.quote: GTR have stated this was not how the train system had been specified to operate and the event should not have caused a permanent lockout fault on the trains. The technical specification for the trains states that the trains will continue to operate with supply frequency drops down to 48.5Hz for short periods of time. All other GTR classes of train were unaffected.
sources.section: 5.2 Critical Infrastructure – Rail

segments.content: ESO 5.2: software change and Siemens patch

sources.quote: The effects were exacerbated as the fleet was undergoing a software change which meant the train drivers could not recover trains which were operating on the new software. The train manufacturer, Siemens, are developing a patch which will allow the drivers to recover the trains themselves without the need for a reboot or technician to attend site. In addition Siemens will investigate how the train could be made to operate for a short time with a supply frequency of 48.5Hz.
sources.section: 5.2 Critical Infrastructure – Rail

segments.content: ESO 5.2: evacuations, cancellations, delays and station closures

sources.quote: The impact to the rail network was that there were 23 train evacuations and thousands of passengers had their journeys delayed with 371 trains cancelled, 220 part cancelled, and 873 trains delayed. London St Pancras and King’s Cross stations had to close for several hours due to overcrowding and London Euston went exit only for a period of time.
sources.section: 5.2 Critical Infrastructure – Rail

segments.content: ESO executive summary: approximately 60 trains, half needed a technician

sources.quote: A major contributor to the disruption relates to a particular class of train operating in the South-East area – approximately 60 trains unexpectedly shut down when the frequency dropped below 49Hz, half of which required a visit from a technician to restart.
sources.section: Executive Summary – Immediate Consequences

segments.content: ESO section 7: approximately 30 trains could not be restarted

sources.quote: The disruption to rail services extended through Friday evening and into Saturday morning due to the fact that approximately 30 trains stopped operating and could not be restarted following the original frequency drop to 49Hz. Restarting them required a technician with a laptop to attend each train which took some time.
sources.section: section 7, Report Findings

segments.content: Part heading: ORR report title and date

sources.quote: Report following railway power disruption on 9th August 2019 3rd January 2020
sources.section: Title page

segments.content: ORR 1.0: event time and frequency as ORR states them

sources.quote: On Friday 9th August 2019 around 4:52pm, a number of electricity generators tripped off the power grid at approximately the same time.
sources.section: 1.0 Introduction

sources.quote: The loss of generation caused the frequency of the power supply to the rail network to drop from its nominal value of 50.0Hz to below 49.0Hz for approximately 33 seconds, falling to a low of 48.8Hz.
sources.section: 1.0 Introduction

sources.quote: The majority of rolling stock operated without any issues.
sources.section: 1.0 Introduction

segments.content: ORR 1.0: 31 stranded, 29 locked out, 22/7, two Class 387, 30 evacuated

sources.quote: However, 31 trains were stranded as a result of the temporary drop in frequency. On the Class 700 and Class 717 rolling stock, protection systems operated within 200ms of the frequency falling to 49.0Hz causing a lock-out of 29 trains. 22 trains were permanently locked-out and could not be reset without a technician attending on site while 7 trains were restored through driver-reset. Two Class 387 trains were also trapped as a result of the lock-out experienced by the Class 700 and Class 717 trains. Passengers had to be evacuated from 30 trains to a place of safety (detrained). There were substantial knock-on delays following recovery of the vehicles.
sources.section: 1.0 Introduction

segments.content: ORR 2.1: frequency description and Figure 1 caption

sources.quote: The supplied power frequency dropped from a nominal 50.0Hz to a low level of 48.8Hz after 16 seconds. The frequency remained below 49.0Hz for approximately 33 seconds and was restored back to its nominal value of 50Hz 3 minutes and 36 seconds later.
sources.section: 2.1 Impact on the quality of power supplied to the railway

sources.quote: Figure 1 – Annotated Frequency Trace of Event [extracted from National Grid Technical Report on the events of 9 August 2019 published 06/08/2019]
sources.section: 2.1 Impact on the quality of power supplied to the railway

segments.content: ORR 2.1: Class 700/717 shut down within 200 ms below 49.0 Hz

sources.quote: The majority of the rolling stock on the network at the time operated without notable issues, but a fleet of Class 700 and Class 717 trains operated by Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) shut down within 200ms of the frequency dropping below 49.0Hz.
sources.section: 2.1 Impact on the quality of power supplied to the railway

segments.content: ORR 2.2: 29 trains locked out; Fleet Control advice

sources.quote: Within 200ms of the power supply frequency dropping below 49.0Hz, 29 trains comprising Class 700 and Class 717, operated by Govia Thameslink Railway, shut down and were locked-out by on-board safety systems. Initial attempts made by drivers to bring the trains back into operation proved abortive and required the intervention of Fleet Control to advise drivers on the next action.
sources.section: 2.2 Effect on GTR's Class 700 and Class 717 fleet

segments.content: ORR 2.2: quotation of GTR's review; 4QC isolation and battery supply

sources.quote: According to a technical review carried out by GTR, ‘all Desiro City Class 700 and 717 units operating on AC Voltage suffered a Protective Shutdown where the converter, known as the 4QC (Four Quadrant Chopper) shut down.’ When the 4QC shuts down, the train is isolated from the traction power supply. Available power is restricted to the limited on-board battery supply, which only supplies certain key on-board systems and does not provide power for traction.
sources.section: 2.2 Effect on GTR's Class 700 and Class 717 fleet

segments.content: ORR 2.2: GSM-R call; 7 recovered, 22 needed a technician

sources.quote: Following the diagnosis of the shutdown by Fleet Control, a GSM-R (Global System for Mobile Communications – Railway) call was broadcast to instruct drivers of affected trains to carry out the Battery Reset Process. The process led to the recovery of 7 of the affected units. 22 trains could not be reset and required the attendance of a technician to recover them.
sources.section: 2.2 Effect on GTR's Class 700 and Class 717 fleet

segments.content: ORR 2.2: 18 technicians sent immediately

sources.quote: At the time of the event, the technicians available were too few compared to the number of stranded trains. 18 Technicians with laptops were sent to restore the trains immediately, and within the next hour more technicians were mobilised.
sources.section: 2.2 Effect on GTR's Class 700 and Class 717 fleet

segments.content: ORR 2.3: recovery, 30 trains detrained, full service within 24 hours

sources.quote: The geographical locations of some of the trains meant they were not easily accessible, making the entire train recovery process time-consuming. Passengers were safely detrained at stations and on track from 30 stranded trains. There were significant train delays, cancellations and part-cancellations of train journeys. However, full service was restored within 24 hours.
sources.section: 2.3 Effects on timetable

segments.content: ORR Table 1: routes, cancellations, part-cancellations, delay minutes

sources.quote: Routes Cancelled Part- Cancelled Delay Minutes Sussex 38 22 2051
sources.section: 2.3, Table 1 – Affected routes, cancellations and delays

sources.quote: Wessex 0 2 716 Kent 36 43 1727 Western 0 0 658 LNE-York 86 44 5569 LNE-EM 197 79 2780 LNW-N 14 24 428 Wales 0 6 499 TOTAL 371 220 14428 Table 1 – Affected routes, cancellations and delays Source: Network Rail’s National Daily Report 09/08/2019
sources.section: 2.3, Table 1 – Affected routes, cancellations and delays

segments.content: ORR 2.5: compensation claims in period 5

sources.quote: There was an increase in delay compensation claims received by train operators in period 5 (21st July to 18th Aug) to the highest level since May 2018 timetable disruption with a particular peak for GTR. Although this cannot be directly attributable to the power disruption, it is likely to have been a factor. There was no corresponding peak in complaints during this time and this remained on trend.
sources.section: 2.5 Possible impact on compensation

segments.content: ORR 3.0: engagement and parties' roles

sources.quote: ORR engaged with Network Rail, GTR and Siemens, to understand the extent of the impact of the power disruption and why it significantly affected the railway services despite not losing traction power. Network Rail owns and manages the railway infrastructure. GTR is a train operating company operating the affected trains and carrying out some of the maintenance. Siemens as the train manufacturer designed the software on the affected trains and also maintains some of the trains.
sources.section: 3.0 Review of Investigations

segments.content: ORR 3.1: permanent vs temporary lock-out definitions

sources.quote: This report refers to a “lock-out” as a situation where a component’s operation has been stopped by a software-based protection system.
sources.section: 3.1 Permanent versus temporary lock-out

sources.quote: Permanent lock-outs are in place to protect against on-board risks with high severity such as fire and electrocution, which could occur when damaged components get reenergised. A permanent lock-out requires a technician with a laptop to physically connect to the train and reset the lock-out.
sources.section: 3.1 Permanent versus temporary lock-out

sources.quote: Temporary lock-outs are in place to protect against risks with low severity following a short-lived system fault or mal-operation. In such cases the train either resets itself as soon as the fault is cleared, or the train driver resets the software system using a Battery Reset Process.
sources.section: 3.1 Permanent versus temporary lock-out

segments.content: ORR 3.1: programmed minimum 49.0 Hz; drive disconnected within 200 ms

sources.quote: All Class 700 and 717 trains had been programmed by Siemens to operate from a power supply of a nominal 50.0Hz, with a minimum frequency of 49.0Hz. When the software detected that the frequency
sources.section: 3.1 Permanent versus temporary lock-out

sources.quote: had dropped below this level, it operated as designed, disconnecting the traction drive within 200ms.
sources.section: 3.1 Permanent versus temporary lock-out

segments.content: ORR 3.1: software 3.25.x temporary vs 3.27.x permanent lock-out

sources.quote: Individual trains within the fleets had different software levels installed, as a software change was being implemented progressively across the fleets. On detecting the frequency drop, the units with software version 3.25.x went into a temporary lock-out while the units with version 3.27.x went into permanent lock-out. The drivers were able to reset units with a temporary lock-out by carrying out a battery reset, while the units with a permanent lockout required a technician to attend to perform a reset.
sources.section: 3.1 Permanent versus temporary lock-out

segments.content: ORR 3.2: why 3.27.x introduced a permanent lock-out

sources.quote: The two software versions reacted differently as the later version 3.27.x software was intended to address what had been identified as a safety risk linked to the earlier software version 3.25.x.
sources.section: 3.2 Implementation of Permanent Lock-out

sources.quote: Siemens identified that there could be circumstances where the Train Control Management System (TCMS) locked out a train system in response to a serious fault or out-of-specification condition that could lead to a safety incident, only for the driver to perform a battery reset. This cleared the lockout and allowed power to be restored to the fault which could make the incident worse.
sources.section: 3.2 Implementation of Permanent Lock-out

sources.quote: Siemens decided to implement a “permanent lock-out” in software version 3.27.x that could not be cleared by a battery reset. Such a permanent lock-out would require a technician to attend the train and perform an analysis of the causes of the lock-out before clearing it.
sources.section: 3.2 Implementation of Permanent Lock-out

sources.quote: Among the conditions selected was the detection of a low power supply frequency.
sources.section: 3.2 Implementation of Permanent Lock-out

segments.content: ORR 3.3: purpose of the lock-out; implications not given weight

sources.quote: The imposition of a lock-out when the supply frequency is outside of specified limits is understood to be a protection against the generation by the 4QC of electromagnetic interference in a range that can affect signalling circuits. Such protection is only required when the power supply is not in the specified frequency range, and therefore the lock-out could be permitted to automatically reset when the supply frequency
sources.section: 3.3 Implications of permanent lock-out

sources.quote: returns to its nominal value.
sources.section: 3.3 Implications of permanent lock-out

sources.quote: the service-disrupting implications of imposing a lock-out requiring a driver or – as in this case – a technician to reset appear not to have been given weight when developing the protection parameters for the on-train software.
sources.section: 3.3 Implications of permanent lock-out

segments.content: ORR 3.3: collective response per design but not explicit intention

sources.quote: Variations in the power supply frequency, however, affect many trains at the same time and result in the same response from all trains that have the same software. It appears therefore that the collective response of the Class 700 and 717 trains to the out-of-specification supply frequency was in accordance with the software design, but was not an explicit intention. Siemens accepts that the temporary reduction in frequency should not have been considered a situation that requires a permanent lock-out.
sources.section: 3.3 Implications of permanent lock-out

segments.content: ORR 3.4: Siemens interim email on original design and hysteresis

sources.quote: In an interim email to ORR, Siemens stated
sources.section: 3.4 Applicable standards

sources.quote: The original design of the class 700 is for the 4QCs to stop pulsing when the line frequency is out of range and automatically restart when the frequency come back in range. This does not require driver action. With the hysteresis implemented, the 4QCs lock when line frequency drops below 49Hz and they restart when the frequency rises above 49.5Hz.
sources.section: 3.4 Applicable standards

segments.content: ORR 4.0: 23 evacuated; delays attributed to permanent lock-out

sources.quote: 23 trains were evacuated without incident.
sources.section: 4.0 Conclusion

sources.quote: The significant delays encountered by most passengers could be attributed to the permanent lock-out of some of the Class 700 and Class 717 trains. Findings so far revealed that TCMS software classed the reduction in frequency as a scenario which required a permanent lock-out.
sources.section: 4.0 Conclusion

segments.content: ORR 4.0: 30 trains on upgraded software stranded

sources.quote: The permanent lock-out resulted in 30 trains running the upgraded software to be effectively stranded on the network and therefore requiring a technician reset. This resulted in significant delays for the entire network and significant knock on effects that lasted beyond the initial incident. However, full service was restored within 24hours.
sources.section: 4.0 Conclusion

segments.content: ORR 4.0: no non-compliance established with the Interoperability Regulations

sources.quote: So far, ORR has not been able to establish any non-compliance with The Railways (Interoperability) Regulations 2011, as amended, that could warrant an enforcement action. The findings are lessons learned that will be fed back for awareness and improvement.
sources.section: 4.0 Conclusion

Ofgem 2.6: 29 trains, two Class 387, 30 evacuated

sources.quote: Publication date: 3 January 2020

sources.quote: In the transport sector, 29 Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR) Class 700 and 717 trains shut down and became stranded when the system frequency fell below 49Hz due to their own on-board automatic frequency protection systems. Two Class 387
sources.section: Section 2, Consequences of the event, 2.6

sources.quote: trains were also trapped by the stranded units, and altogether passengers had to be safely evacuated from 30 trains.
sources.section: Section 2, Consequences of the event, 2.6

segments.content: Ofgem 2.7: 22 permanently locked out; software update

sources.quote: Some of these protection settings were reset by the driver but 22 permanently locked out and had to be reset by a technician, which was the main cause of disruption to rail lines into St Pancras International and King’s Cross. A software update is being introduced to these trains so that they can be automatically reset if the frequency drops below 49Hz in the future.
sources.section: Section 2, Consequences of the event, 2.7

segments.content: Ofgem 2.9 and executive summary: cancellations; more than 500 services disrupted

sources.quote: As a result, there was significant disruption to the rail network, with 371 services cancelled and 220 part cancelled.
sources.section: Section 2, Consequences of the event, 2.9

sources.quote: The rail services were particularly affected with more than 500 services disrupted.
sources.section: Executive Summary

segments.content: E3C interim: 60 trains, around half restarted, 371 cancelled, 873 delayed

sources.quote: The Department for Transport confirmed that rail commuters experienced significant disruption due to a safety mechanism built-in to all operational Class 700 and Class 717 Desiro City trains. This detected the drop in frequency on the electricity system which triggered 60 trains to shut down
sources.section: Impact on Essential Services, Rail

sources.quote: While around half of the affected trains were restarted by their drivers, the rest required engineers to be dispatched, blocking tracks and causing huge disruption on lines into St Pancras International and King’s Cross. 371 services were cancelled and 873 delayed,
sources.section: Impact on Essential Services, Rail

sources.quote: This led to St Pancras International, King’s Cross and Euston stations having to limit passenger numbers entering the stations at various times.
sources.section: Impact on Essential Services, Rail

segments.content: E3C interim: trains out of position; delays into 11 August

sources.quote: a number of trains did not end up in their correct location at the end of the day, which led to some early morning services on Saturday 10 th August being disrupted.
sources.section: Impact on Essential Services, Rail

sources.quote: This is especially true for rail services which experienced major delays that extended into Sunday 11th August.
sources.section: Executive Summary

sources.quote: The Class 700 and 717 trains, have been introduced over the last three years
sources.section: Impact on Essential Services, Rail

segments.content: E3C final section 4: rail disruption figures

sources.quote: Energy Emergencies Executive Committee (E3C): Final report January 2020
sources.section: Title page

sources.quote: The rail sector reported disruptions because Thameslink class 700 and 717 trains systems were overprotective to frequency drops on the electricity network and shut down. A number of trains required manual engineer intervention to restart trains and the complexity of the restart process caused significant disruptions translating to 371 cancelled services, 220 part cancelled services and 873 delayed services.
sources.section: chapter 4, Impact on essential services
